title: Prison (Genesis 39–40)
hook: a false accusation, prison, and a forgotten favor

segments.voice: Yesterday, into the pit, bor: the brothers stripped Joseph's coat, dropped him in a dry cistern, and sold him to traders bound for Egypt. Your line was sold by his own. Who did you hold in prayer? Day three hundred sixty-two.

Egypt. Joseph is a slave now, still a young man, bought by an officer of Pharaoh named Potiphar. And something odd happens: everything he touches goes well. Before long he's running the whole house. Then his master's wife starts noticing him, day after day, and one day, when no one else is inside, she grabs him by his cloak. He runs, and leaves the cloak in her hand. That's twice now a piece of Joseph's clothing has been turned into a lie. His brothers dipped his coat in goat's blood. She holds up his cloak and says he attacked her. Potiphar believes her. Joseph goes to prison. Today: the prison, and the sentence the text keeps repeating there.
screen: `A SLAVE IN POTIPHAR'S HOUSE.` → `A CLOAK LEFT IN HER HAND.` → `PRISON.`

segments.voice: Read chapter thirty-nine slowly and one phrase keeps coming back: the Lord was with Joseph. It's there when he's a slave in Potiphar's house. It's there when his master sees everything prospering in his hands. And it's there twice in the prison. "But the Lord was with Joseph," the Douay-Rheims reads, and soon the keeper of the prison puts him in charge of all the other prisoners. Notice where the sentence shows up. Not on the day he's made governor. In the slave quarters and in the cell. The text never says God got him out. It says God was with him in it. Second, what Joseph does when no one is looking. He refused his master's wife, and he gave two reasons: it would betray the man who trusted him with everything, and it would be a sin against God. Nobody was watching. That was the whole test. Third, the forgotten favor. Two of Pharaoh's officials land in the same prison: the chief butler, who poured Pharaoh's wine, and the chief baker. Each has a dream. Joseph sees their faces are sad one morning and asks why. He says interpretations belong to God, then tells them: in three days the butler goes back to his post, and the baker dies. Both come true. Joseph asks one thing of the butler: remember me to Pharaoh. And the chapter ends flatly. The butler forgot him. Two full years go by. Centuries later, a psalm looks back on this stretch of his life: his feet humbled in fetters, iron around him, until God's word came. Two years is a long time to be forgotten. The chapter doesn't hurry past it, and it never calls the waiting wasted.
screen: `THE LORD WAS WITH JOSEPH, IN THE CELL.` · `HE SAID NO WHEN NO ONE WAS WATCHING.` · `REMEMBER ME. THE BUTLER FORGOT.` · `A PSALM REMEMBERS THE FETTERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one right thing no one will see. Settle, and breathe. Walk through the rest of your day and find the moments nobody's checking: the dishes in the sink, the receipt that's slightly wrong in your favor, what you say about someone who isn't in the room. Pick one. Picture yourself doing the right thing there, quietly, with no credit and no audience. If you pray, you can carry the phrase from the chapter: the Lord was with Joseph. If you don't, just hold the choice for a minute and let it settle. The bell holds the time.
Prison. In Genesis, the place Joseph lands on a false charge, and where the text says, twice, the Lord was with him. Today's word.
Your line: the lord was with joseph. Today, somewhere no one's watching, do the right thing anyway, and let it stay unseen. Day three hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: The Joseph story is read at Mass on a weekday in Lent, and Psalm 105 (104 in the Douay numbering), which remembers Joseph in fetters, is among the psalms of the Liturgy of the Hours.

original.note: Hebrew: the prison in Joseph's story. the word sohar is rare outside these chapters, and its exact sense is uncertain.

trapdoor: what you thought: a bad chapter before the good part.
what it means: a slave, then a prisoner on a false charge, and the text keeps saying the Lord was with him there.
what a scholar hears: the phrase frames Genesis 39 from the house to the cell, and the prison gets a rare Hebrew name, beit ha-sohar.

sources.quoted: But the Lord was with Joseph

notes: 'The Lord was with Joseph/him' appears in some form at Genesis 39:2, 39:3, 39:21 and 39:23; the script says 'twice in the prison' (39:21, 39:23). Confirm against the Douay-Rheims wording.
Joseph's two reasons for refusing (betraying his master's trust; sin against God) paraphrase Genesis 39:8–9.
Beit ha-sohar (Genesis 39:20–23; 40:3, 5): the sense of sohar ('round house'?) is debated; confirm the note.

Joseph as a type of Christ is a standard patristic and Catholic reading; howItsDone says the Joseph story is read at weekday Mass in Lent (Genesis 37 on the Friday of the second week of Lent in the current lectionary). Reviewer changed 'on weekdays in Lent' to 'on a weekday in Lent' to match that single reading. Confirm.
